quotes.text: Well, it is a tremendously important issue, in the sense that we know that there are a lot of questions about the use of AI, huge benefits, huge opportunities, huge challenges, too. And I will say NTIA right now has a fairly limited portfolio in this space at the moment, but we do serve as the President's adviser on telecommunications and information policy. There is very active work happening within the Administration at the OSTP and the White House. Our colleagues at NIST are working on artificial intelligence. And I will say that we stand ready to assist those efforts as needed. Just as an observation, I will just say this is an area where American leadership is quite important, as others start to move into the space.

Well, it is a terrific question. So I will just say just generally, I mean, we are excited about responsible innovation in AI, right? [...] there are these real risks and concerns that need to be addressed if we are going to have a successful deployment of AI.
we are only going to be able to get this right if we are dealing with the risks and the benefits here.

One pressing issue is the advancement of artificial intelligence systems. [...] Responsible AI innovation will bring enormous benefits, but only if we address the real risks and harms that it poses. [...] That is why NTIA is seeking public feedback on what policies can support the development of AI audits and assessments to create earned trust in AI.

When you think about AI and the language models that are used, how do you know what the primary sources are? [...] When you look at the algorithm, you just know what got—you don't really get to see what was filtered. So, Mr. Fang, Ms. Richardson, do you have thoughts about how we detect this kind of activity in AI?

You could see how AI could do a lot of the work of analytics, could do a lot of the work of the code, and might even be able to accelerate or lower the bar for the skill needed in the math, so it could change that function. [...] How are we going to use AI to solve problems that are not getting adequately solved yet today?

we are working on outbound investment. So I wonder, Mr. Nemeroff, as you think about AI, in particular, one of the most rapidly changing tech sectors and you think about cyber and other factors, what kinds of things ought we to consider within cybersecurity?
I truly believe this poses an existential threat to Western civilization. [...] It is the kind of power that the Death Star has over civilization.

Because we are serious about fostering innovation, and we are serious about our Constitution, we also need to recognize that AI should serve the American people without turning it into another tool for unchecked surveillance or data exploitation.
Without it, we are handing the keys over to a surveillance state on steroids. [...] We cannot let AI become another excuse for Big Brother to pry into our lives.

Mr. Cohen, there is a lot of discussion about the importance of winning the AI race against China. Frankly, I am concerned—to beat China, we should not try to be more like China. I do not want to be like China. I want to be like America but yes, on the technology end, we want to win the AI race. [...] Can you give us a sense of how you view this discussion through the lens of our capital markets and give us your perspective on the level of AI adoption Nasdaq is seeing from the broader market and China in particular?
